newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten says rolling back HK liberties disturbing.
newsitem.headline: Patten says rolling back HK liberties disturbing.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten said on Saturday the move by a China committee to roll back civil liberties in the territory after Beijing takes over on July 1 was "disturbing".

"Once again we have the impression of legal arguments hastily thrown together, policies made up as we go along," Patten said in a statement in response to the 150-member Preparatory Committee's decision to repeal civil liberties laws in Hong Kong after the handover.

"The community is not naive. Many will now be concluding that the freedoms protected by the provisions in question are deemed to be "against the Basic Law' because it has been decided for reasons which have nothing to do with the Basic Law that those freedoms should be reduced," he said.
Patten challenged the China-anointed caucus, which is responsible for shaping Hong Kong's future after the handover, to explain to the 6.3 million Hong Kong people the motive behind the changes.

Hong Kong will return to China at midnight on June 30, ending more than 150 years of colonial rule. China has promised Hong Kong will maintain a high degree of autonomy and keep its capitalistic way of life intact for 50 years after the changing of sovereignty.
The Basic Law will serve as the territory's post-colonial constitution.

Patten also criticised the proposal by the committee to "legitimise" the controversial provisional legislature, which will be installed at the stroke of midnight on June 30 to reverse his political reform by replacing the current elected Legislative Council.

"This looks like a belated recognition that this body has a legitmacy problem," he said. "But no amount of retrospective tinkering can change the reality of that this is a questionable body established for questionable motives to do questionable work."
